slides.title: Morphology
slides.content: Morphology Morphemes The smallest unit of meaning. Stem: supplies the main meaning Also called lemma, base form, root, lexeme Aﬃx: adds additional meaning Morphemes Bound: Cannot appear as a word by itself s (dog-s), ly (quick-ly), ed (walk-ed) Free: Can appear as a word by itself, may combine with other morphemes of, the, dog (dog-s), walk (walk-ed) 7 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Morphology
slides.content: Morphology Inﬂectional morphemes • Examples: dog (NOUN) + s = dogs (NOUN) eat (VERB) + s = eats (VERB) eat (VERB) + ing = eating (VERB) • Bound morphemes used to make grammatical distinctions • Change the form of the word but not its POS tag or key meaning 8 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Morphology
slides.content: Morphology Derivational morphemes • Examples: appoint (VERB) + ee = appointee (NOUN) help (VERB) + less = helpless (ADJ) strength (NOUN) + en = strengthen (VERB) • Bound morphemes used to create new words • Change the form, POS tag and meaning of the word 9 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Morphology
slides.content: Morphology Concatenative morphology Stem + aﬃx(es). Aﬃxes • Preﬁxes: disestablish • Suﬃxes: establishment Can be combined: disestablishment 10 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Morphology
slides.content: Morphology Non-concatenative morphology Inﬁxes: e.g., Tagalog: hingi (borrow) →humingi (borrower) Circumﬁxes e.g., German: sagen (say) →gesagt (said) Reduplication e.g., Motu: mahuta (to sleep) →mahutamahuta (to sleep constantly) 11 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Morphology
slides.content: Morphology Morphological typology Languages vary in how they use morphology English: We learned these new words Chinese: Wˇomen xué le zhè xi sh¯engcí I.PL.AN learn .PAST this .PL new word Russian: My vyučili eti novyje slova We.NOM learn.PAST.PL this.ACC.PL new.ACC.PL word.ACC.PL • Russian (synthetic) has more morphemes per word than Chinese (isolating) • English is in between, it’s a continuum Examples borrowed from Kat Vyloma 12 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Morphology
slides.content: Morphology Morphological typology Languages on a continuum of morphemes per word, estimated by Greenberg (1960), ﬁgure by Jurafsky and Martin (2025) 13 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Morphology
slides.content: Morphology Morphological typology West Greenlandic (polysynthetic) Nannu-n-niuti-kkuminar-tu-rujussu-u-vuq polar.bear-catch-instrument.for.achieving-something.good.for- PART-big-be-3SG.INDIC It (a dog) is really good for catching polar bears with. Example from Fortescue (2017) 14 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Morphology
slides.content: Morphology Morphological typology Agglutinative: Morphemes have one meaning (e.g. Turkish) Fusional: Morphemes may have multiple meanings (e.g. Russian) This is also a continuum 15 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Morphology
slides.content: Morphology Morphological typology • Agglutinative and fusional languages are more morphologically complex than isolating languages • Large consensus that morphologically complex languages are underserved by current NLP models • Ongoing research on: • quantifying and explaining the diﬃculty, e.g. Park et al. (2021); Poelman et al. (2025) • addressing the inequality, e.g. Ataman et al. (2020) 16 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Rule-based morphological processing
slides.content: Rule-based morphological processing Finite-state automaton (FSA) An abstract machine used to recognize patterns in input sequences. (Used also to implement regular expressions, see lecture 2) A FSA for English nominal inﬂection (Jurafsky and Martin, 2009) 26 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Rule-based morphological processing
slides.content: Rule-based morphological processing Needs • A list of stems (reg-noun) • A list of singular and plural irregular nouns →A lexicon A FSA for English nominal inﬂection (Jurafsky and Martin, 2009) 26 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Rule-based morphological processing
slides.content: Rule-based morphological processing A FSA for English verbal inﬂection (Jurafsky and Martin, 2009) reg-verb-stem: walk fry talk irreg-verb-stem: catch speak sing irreg-past-verb-form: caught spoke sang • walk + past = walked • walk + present participle = walking • walk + 3sg = walks 27 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Rule-based morphological processing
slides.content: Rule-based morphological processing A FSA for English nominal inﬂection (Jurafsky and Martin, 2009) 28 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Rule-based morphological processing
slides.content: Rule-based morphological processing Use of FSAs • Word recognition • Helpfulness • Helpfully • Helpfulization • Generalized to Finite State Transducers (FSTs) • Morphological analysis • Morphological generation 29 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Rule-based morphological processing
slides.content: Rule-based morphological processing Limitations of FSAs • Require linguistic annotation which is costly • Need to be updated when new words appear in the vocabulary • Cannot handle reduplication where arbitrarily long sequences are copied We won’t see more details. See Chapter 3 of Jurafsky and Martin (2009) if you are interested. 30 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Data-driven morphological processing
slides.content: Data-driven morphological processing Morphological analysis • Most tasks in morphological analysis can be framed as word-level tagging tasks • Tagging models can be applied directly (see lecture 6) Lemma Morphology Le le Deﬁnite=Def|Gender=Masc|Number=Sing chat chat Gender=Masc|Number=Sing chasse chasser Mood=Ind|Number=Sing|Person=3|Tense=Pres|VerbForm=Fin les le Deﬁnite=Def|Gender=Masc|Number=Sing chiens chien Gender=Masc|Number=Plur . . _ 32 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Data-driven morphological processing
slides.content: Data-driven morphological processing Multitask architecture for joint POS, morphology, lemma tagging and dependency parsing (Kondratyuk and Straka, 2019). 33 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Data-driven morphological processing
slides.content: Data-driven morphological processing Tagging in Kondratyuk and Straka (2019) • Input representation: word represented using a transformer • Passed to a softmax • Argmax of softmax is selected as tag 34 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Data-driven morphological processing
slides.content: Data-driven morphological processing Morphological analysis as tagging • Tasks learned sequentially: lemmatizing →POS tagging →morphology jointly: Multi-task learning • Morphological tags: all-in-one: Tag: Mood=Ind|Number=Sing|Person=3|Tense=Pres|VerbForm=Fin split: Tag 1: Mood=Ind, Tag 2: Number=Sing etc. In practice, joint learning of all-in-one category works best. 35 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Data-driven morphological processing
slides.content: Data-driven morphological processing Instead of using an encoder architecture, some of these tasks can be modelled with an encoder-decoder architecture. 36 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Data-driven morphological processing
slides.content: Data-driven morphological processing Visualization of the diﬀerent NN architectures for sequence processing. See lecture 4. 37 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Data-driven morphological processing
slides.content: Data-driven morphological processing Encoder-decoder architecture for lemmatization (Kanerva et al., 2021). The model exploits character-level information and reduces sparsity. 38 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Data-driven morphological processing
slides.content: Data-driven morphological processing Morphological generation For morphological generation tasks, the encoder-decoder (or sequence-to-sequence paradigm) can be applied. 39 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Data-driven morphological processing
slides.content: Data-driven morphological processing Seq2seq model for inﬂection generation. The model produces the simple past form of the verb dun (Senuma and Aizawa, 2017). 40 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Data-driven morphological processing
slides.content: Data-driven morphological processing Evaluation and SOTA • Evaluation metric: depends on task but usually word-level accuracy • SOTA for morphological analysis: lower than POS tagging with more variation (∼50 to 95 if enough data) • Even more language dependent • Check out more on sigmorphon if you are interested 41 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Morphologically-informed subword tokenization
slides.content: Morphologically-informed subword tokenization Remember BPE? (Lecture 2) Corpus 5 l o w _ 2 l o w e s t _ 6 n e w er_ 3 w i d er_ 2 n e w _ Vocabulary _, d, e, i, l, n, o, r, s, t, w, er, er_ First merge e r →er Second merge er _ →er_ 43 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Morphologically-informed subword tokenization
slides.content: Morphologically-informed subword tokenization Representing BPE merges as a tree newer_ new ne n e w er_ er e r _ Merge rules M1 (e, r) M2 (er, _) M3 (n, e) M4 (ne, w) M7 (new, er_) 44 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Morphologically-informed subword tokenization
slides.content: Morphologically-informed subword tokenization So the tree for independently should look roughly like this, right? independently independent in i n dependent depend de d e pend p p pend en e n d ent en e n t ly l y Imaginary BPE tree consistent with morphological boundaries. 45 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Morphologically-informed subword tokenization
slides.content: Morphologically-informed subword tokenization Well... ˙Gindependently ˙Gindepend ˙Gind ˙Gin ˙G in i n d epend ep e p end en e n d ently ent en e n t ly l y RoBERTa BPE tree, generated with the TkTkT library by Thomas Bauwens. 46 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Morphologically-informed subword tokenization
slides.content: Morphologically-informed subword tokenization • You might say it does not matter if the end result is consistent with morphological boundaries • But in some cases it is not BPE tree of the word horseshoe by RoBERTa 47 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Morphologically-informed subword tokenization
slides.content: Morphologically-informed subword tokenization • BPE segments text deterministically • Some morphemes like ly may be in the vocabulary but underused in segmentation ⇒undertrained • Limits compositional generalization: • initially • inherentently • dependable 48 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Morphologically-informed subword tokenization
slides.content: Morphologically-informed subword tokenization What can we do about it? ˙Gindependently ˙Gindepend ? ˙Gin ˙G ? i n d epend ep e p ? en e n d ? ent ? e n t ly l y BPE-dropout (Provilkov et al., 2020) • Randomly disable merges (temporarily) • Can produce multiple segmentations of the same input • Empirically improves downstream performance 49 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Morphologically-informed subword tokenization
slides.content: Morphologically-informed subword tokenization What can we do about it? ˙Gindependently ˙Gindepend ˙Gin ˙G in i n d epend ep e p end en e n d ent en e n t ly l y BPE-knockout (Bauwens and Delobelle, 2024) • Disable bad merges • Bad merges are determined based on a morphological lexicon • Outperforms BPE-dropout downstream 50 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Morphologically-informed subword tokenization
slides.content: Morphologically-informed subword tokenization BPE-knockout result for independently ˙Gin ˙G in i n dependent depend d epend ep e p end en e n d ent en e n t ly l y BPE-knockout tree, generated with the TkTkT library by Thomas Bauwens. 51 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Morphologically-informed subword tokenization
slides.content: Morphologically-informed subword tokenization BPE-knockout conclusion • Morphological information can be used to inform subword tokenization • This improves downstream performance • Disadvantage: relies on handcrafted lexicon • Still room for improvement 52 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Summary
slides.content: Summary Summary • Morphology: the study of the internal structure of words • Morphological processing tasks: tagging and generation • FSAs: rule-based methods applied to these tasks • Neural network based methods • How to inform subword tokenization using morphology 54 NLP: Morphological processing

slides.title: Summary
slides.content: Summary Outlook • Direct use of morphology is no longer relevant for English • May still be relevant for languages with more complex morphology • Models of morphological processing can still be improved for some languages • Indirect use of morphology in subword tokenization holds promise even for English 55 NLP: Morphological processing
